subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 74-year-old man reports progressive dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food with a gurgling sound, and foul breath. A barium swallow shows a posterior outpouching just above the cricopharyngeal muscle. He has noticed a soft neck mass that gurgles when compressed. Histology of the resected pouch shows mucosa and submucosa only.
question: Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this lesion?

options.text: Persistent vitelline duct forming a true diverticulum of the ileum
Increased colonic intraluminal pressure with vasa recta penetration
Esophageal dysmotility causing mucosal herniation through Killian triangle
Failure of neural crest migration to a distal colonic segment
Atherosclerotic hypoperfusion of the bowel wall

explanation_correct: This is Zenker diverticulum, a pharyngoesophageal false diverticulum in which esophageal dysmotility causes herniation of mucosa and submucosa through an area of weakness (Killian triangle) between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal parts of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor. It is most common in older males and causes dysphagia, obstruction, gurgling, aspiration, foul breath, and a neck mass. The lack of a muscularis layer confirms it is a false diverticulum.

explanation_incorrect.A: A persistent vitelline duct produces Meckel diverticulum, a true diverticulum of the terminal ileum, not a pharyngoesophageal pouch in an older man.
explanation_incorrect.B: Colonic pressure with vasa recta penetration produces colonic false diverticula (diverticulosis), not a hypopharyngeal outpouching.
explanation_incorrect.D: Failed neural crest migration causes Hirschsprung disease, an aganglionic colon presenting in infancy, not a cervical diverticulum.
explanation_incorrect.E: Atherosclerotic hypoperfusion causes mesenteric ischemia with postprandial pain, not a mucosal outpouching at the pharyngoesophageal junction.

educationalObjective: Zenker diverticulum is a false diverticulum from dysmotility with mucosal herniation through Killian triangle between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal muscles.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 70-year-old man with a long-standing Zenker diverticulum begins coughing and choking on food at night and develops a productive cough with fever. He also notes that food particles and saliva collect in the pouch and are regurgitated hours after eating, with a gurgling noise and foul-smelling breath.
question: Which of the following symptoms is a recognized consequence of this diverticulum retaining food and secretions?

options.text: Aspiration with recurrent pulmonary symptoms
Painless hematochezia from ectopic gastric mucosa
Currant jelly stools from intussusception
Pneumaturia from a fistula to the bladder
Bilious emesis from a midgut volvulus

explanation_correct: A Zenker diverticulum retains food and saliva, leading to regurgitation, gurgling, foul breath, and—because material can spill into the airway—aspiration, which can produce recurrent pulmonary symptoms such as coughing and fever. This is why aspiration is listed among its classic presenting symptoms along with dysphagia, obstruction, and neck mass.

explanation_incorrect.B: Painless hematochezia from ectopic gastric mucosa is a feature of Meckel diverticulum in the ileum, not a pharyngeal pouch.
explanation_incorrect.C: Currant jelly stools result from intussusception with vascular compromise, typically in infants, not from a Zenker diverticulum.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pneumaturia indicates a colovesical fistula, a complication of diverticulitis in the sigmoid colon, not a cervical diverticulum.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bilious emesis with midgut volvulus is seen in malrotation of infants, not in an older adult with a pharyngoesophageal outpouching.

educationalObjective: Retained food and secretions in a Zenker diverticulum cause dysphagia, gurgling, foul breath, and aspiration.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 2-year-old child undergoes surgery for an ileal outpouching found during evaluation of painless rectal bleeding. Histology confirms the presence of all layers of the bowel wall in the specimen, including muscularis externa and serosa, and ectopic acid-secreting gastric mucosa within the pouch.
question: Which embryologic event is responsible for this lesion?

options.text: Herniation of mucosa through Killian triangle due to dysmotility
High-pressure outpouching where vasa recta pierce the muscularis
Failure of the gut to rotate around the superior mesenteric artery
Persistence of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct
Failure of neural crest cells to migrate into the distal bowel

explanation_correct: This is Meckel diverticulum, a true diverticulum (all wall layers present) resulting from persistence of the vitelline, or omphalomesenteric, duct. It may contain ectopic acid-secreting gastric mucosa and/or pancreatic tissue, which explains painless hematochezia from ulceration of adjacent ileal mucosa. It is the most common congenital anomaly of the GI tract.

explanation_incorrect.A: Herniation through Killian triangle due to dysmotility is Zenker diverticulum, a false pharyngeal diverticulum of older adults, not an ileal true diverticulum.
explanation_incorrect.B: High-pressure outpouching where vasa recta pierce muscle creates acquired colonic false diverticula, not a congenital ileal lesion with all layers.
explanation_incorrect.C: Failure of midgut rotation around the superior mesenteric artery causes malrotation with Ladd bands, not a persistent duct with gastric mucosa.
explanation_incorrect.E: Failed neural crest migration causes Hirschsprung disease, an aganglionic segment of distal colon, not a vitelline duct remnant.

educationalObjective: Meckel diverticulum is a true diverticulum caused by persistence of the vitelline duct and may contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic mucosa.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A clinician is counseling the parents of a child just diagnosed with a symptomatic ileal diverticulum containing gastric mucosa. She reviews the classic 'rule of 2s' that characterizes this anomaly: it occurs twice as often in males, is about 2 inches long, sits about 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, and is found in about 2% of the population.
question: Which of the following completes the 'rule of 2s' for this lesion?

options.text: Presents in the second decade and contains two muscle layers
Commonly presents in the first 2 years of life and may contain 2 types of epithelia
Is 2 cm wide and causes symptoms in 2% of affected individuals
Occurs in 2% of males only and is 2 feet from the cecum
Has 2 layers of mucosa and presents after age 20 in most cases

explanation_correct: The 'rule of 2s' for Meckel diverticulum includes: 2 times as likely in males, 2 inches long, 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, 2% of the population, commonly presenting in the first 2 years of life, and possibly containing 2 types of epithelia (gastric and pancreatic). Option B correctly states two of these—presentation in the first 2 years and two epithelial types.

explanation_incorrect.A: Presentation is classically in the first 2 years of life, not the second decade, and the two epithelia refer to gastric and pancreatic mucosa, not muscle layers.
explanation_incorrect.C: The rule uses 2 inches in length and 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, not a 2-cm width, and the 2% refers to population prevalence, not the fraction of affected individuals who become symptomatic.
explanation_incorrect.D: The lesion occurs 2 times as often in males, not exclusively in males, and its distance is 2 feet from the ileocecal valve rather than the cecum.
explanation_incorrect.E: Meckel diverticulum is a true diverticulum with all layers, not two layers of mucosa, and it most often presents in the first 2 years rather than after age 20.

educationalObjective: Meckel diverticulum follows the rule of 2s: 2× males, 2 inches long, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, 2% of people, first 2 years, 2 epithelia.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 3-year-old boy presents with painless bright red blood per rectum and mild RLQ pain but no fever. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows focal uptake in the right lower abdomen, near the terminal ileum. The bleeding is attributed to a congenital ileal diverticulum containing heterotopic tissue.
question: Which of the following best explains both the positive scan and the painless bleeding in this child?

options.text: A colonic false diverticulum bleeding from a vasa recta vessel
An intussusception with a Meckel diverticulum as the lead point
A Zenker diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa in the neck
Ischemic bowel from embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery
Ectopic acid-secreting gastric mucosa in a Meckel diverticulum taking up pertechnetate

explanation_correct: A technetium-99m pertechnetate (Meckel) scan detects uptake by heterotopic gastric mucosa. In a Meckel diverticulum, ectopic acid-secreting gastric mucosa secretes acid that ulcerates the adjacent ileal mucosa, producing painless hematochezia or melena. The scan's focal RLQ uptake near the terminal ileum localizes the ectopic mucosa and explains both the positive study and the bleeding.

explanation_incorrect.A: A colonic false diverticulum bleeding from vasa recta is painless hematochezia of diverticulosis in older adults, not a pertechnetate-avid ileal lesion in a child.
explanation_incorrect.B: Intussusception with a Meckel lead point causes intermittent pain and currant jelly stools; it would not produce the focal pertechnetate uptake described, which reflects gastric mucosa rather than telescoped bowel.
explanation_incorrect.C: Zenker diverticulum is a pharyngoesophageal false diverticulum in older males, not an abdominal source of bleeding in a child.
explanation_incorrect.D: Embolic SMA occlusion causes acute mesenteric ischemia with pain out of proportion in patients with atrial fibrillation or vascular disease, not a positive Meckel scan.

educationalObjective: A Meckel scan uses 99mTc-pertechnetate uptake by ectopic gastric mucosa to detect a Meckel diverticulum causing painless bleeding.
